name: Graph Golf (order/degree and host-switch problems): beat a 2021 best diameter and average shortest path length
compute_profile: laptop-days (bit-parallel BFS; one exact evaluation of the n = 158976 instance takes minutes on a multi-core laptop)
statement: Graph Golf ran from 2015 to 2021 at the National Institute of Informatics. Given a fixed vertex count and degree bound, it ranks graphs by diameter and then average shortest-path length. Its host-switch variant instead measures paths between degree-one hosts subject to switch port bounds. The archived 2021 graphs include contributions by Team RK, EvbCFfp1XB, D. Shimizu, SDKY-NITTYM and MODAL-Team. The target is a strict lexicographic improvement for an eligible featured cell. Recompute averages from the published edge files as exact fractions. Exclude n40d5 and n432d12, which meet their lower bounds. Later published graphs and valid compositions are part of the comparison.
success_criterion: Success means an explicit graph for one of the 2021 featured problems other than n40d5 and n432d12 (which meet the lower bound), satisfying the definition on http://research.nii.ac.jp/graphgolf/problem.html (general: simple, undirected, connected, exactly n vertices, every degree <= d; host-switch: exactly n hosts of degree 1, each adjacent to a switch, any number of switches of degree <= r, simple and connected), whose (diameter, ASPL), or (h-diameter, h-ASPL), is lexicographically STRICTLY smaller (direction: min) than the best graph listed for that problem on http://research.nii.ac.jp/graphgolf/ranking.html, with the incumbent's ASPL recomputed exactly (total distance divided by the number of pairs, as a rational number) from its published edge file rather than read from the 5-decimal display, and also smaller than any later published graph for that problem. Ties do not count. Include the best valid composition of published objects for the same parameters and metric in the bar, even if it is absent from a printed table. State whether the candidate is a composition. Identify its components and composition rule. Values in unmerged pull requests are not bars.

partial_wins.statement: A strict improvement, under that year's rules and verified the same way, on a featured problem of the 2015-2019 Graph Golf competitions (their ranking pages on the same site), against the best graph listed there and any later published one.

verification_method: Read the edge list (calibrate the format by recomputing an incumbent from its published edges.gz file). Check vertex and host counts, simplicity, degree or radix bounds and connectivity. Run BFS from every vertex (bit-parallel BFS for large n; the organisers link Ryuhei Mori's C++ ASPL program and Ryota Yasudo's host-switch program from problem.html) to get the exact diameter and the exact sum of distances, and compare with the incumbent as rationals. Seconds for small cells, minutes for n = 158976. Recompute comparison compositions using the same checker and resource metric.
status_checked: 2026-10-14; historical source check from supplied batch A material. Current sources were not re-fetched during preparation.
angles: Start from the published incumbents and run degree-preserving edge-swap local search with an incremental bit-parallel ASPL evaluator; most cells saw only two serious teams over one season, five years ago.

For the large structured cells (n65536d64, n100000d128, n158976d10) use algebraic seeds such as Cayley graphs, lifts of small optimal graphs and voltage graphs; vertex-transitive candidates need only one BFS per orbit to evaluate.

For n1024d5 and n3602d24 the prize is a smaller diameter: check the degree-diameter tables for degree-5 diameter-5 and degree-24 diameter-3 graphs of at least that order, and try vertex deletion or merging while keeping the diameter. Any such graph beats every 2021 entry outright.
Host-switch cells with small radix (h32r4, h80r6) are small enough for exhaustive or SAT-assisted search over switch topologies, which could improve the incumbent or show it is optimal.
pitfalls: The 5-decimal ASPL display hides near-ties; recompute both graphs exactly.
Diameter is compared first: a lower ASPL at a larger diameter loses.
General graphs allow degree <= d (not necessarily regular). Hosts must have exactly one edge, to a switch. Multi-edges and loops are not allowed.

The competition is closed, so the organisers will not list a new record. The claim stands against the frozen 2021 table, and a novelty search ('order/degree problem', 'host-switch graph', 2022-2026) is part of it.
Cells whose gap is 0 are optimal and cannot be beaten; a result below a lower bound means a bug.
